lines.text: Welcome back. Last time, we planned our game on paper.
Today, we start building.
And we start with the first question on our plan. What exists?
HTML creates the things that exist in our game.
Here's the starter project you downloaded.
Three files, and you already know their jobs.
index dot html holds the pieces. style dot css makes them look good. And script dot js makes them do things.
To see our game, double-click index dot html, and it opens in your browser.
Right now? A blank page. Let's fix that.
Let's open index dot html.
The top part, called the head, is information about the page. You don't see it. It connects our font, and our CSS file.
Down here is the body. That's what you do see.
And inside it, is one empty box, called game. Every piece of our game goes in here.
See this grey text? That's a comment. The browser ignores it. It's a note for us.
And look. It's our paper plan, written as a to-do list.
HTML is made of tags.
An opening tag. Some content. And a closing tag, with a slash.
Think of tags as labelled boxes. The label tells the browser what kind of thing is inside.
Let's add our first piece. The title.
h1 means heading number one. The biggest heading.
Save the file. Refresh the browser. And there's our title.
Remember this loop. Save, refresh. You'll do it a hundred times.
Next, the score.
A div is a general-purpose box. A span is a small box, for a bit of text.
And see this? id equals score. An id is a name tag.
Later, JavaScript will say, find the thing called score, and change its number. Without a name, it can't find it.
Now the world. An empty box called game area.
You can't see it yet, because it's empty, and it has no style. But it's there.
Everything in the game world goes inside this box. Boxes inside boxes. That's called nesting.
Now let's fill the world.
Two clouds. The player. The obstacle. And the ground.
Save. Refresh. And... nothing?
They're empty boxes, with no size and no colour, so they're invisible. That's CSS's job, next video. But they exist.
Here's a creator trick. Right-click, and choose Inspect. Hover over player... and there it is. It exists.
Notice the clouds use class, not id. An id is for one unique thing. There's only one player. A class is for a group. We can have lots of clouds.
Now, the start message. p means paragraph. A line of text that tells the player how to begin.
And finally, the end of the game. A Game Over heading, and a real button you can click.
We gave this box a class called hidden. Right now, it does nothing. It's still showing.
Next video, CSS will hide it. And in video four, JavaScript will show it at exactly the right moment.
It doesn't look like a game yet.
But compare it to our plan. The dinosaur. The obstacle. The score. The restart button.
Every single thing we drew now exists.
That's what HTML does. It doesn't make things pretty, and it doesn't make them move. It makes them exist.
Before the next video, check your page has everything on this list.
If something's missing, compare your code with the checkpoint file.
Mini challenge. Change the title to your own game's name. And change the button text.
Next time, we take these plain pieces, and make them look like a real game. With CSS.
